newsitem.title: FRANCE: MATIF launches new contracts in battle for trade.
newsitem.headline: MATIF launches new contracts in battle for trade.

text.p: French futures and options exchange MATIF launched seven new contracts on Friday based on European bonds as part of its strategy to capture business from rival exchanges before and after the introduction of a single European currency.

MATIF launched a five-year French franc bond future which will start trading in September and futures and options contracts on five-year German bonds, similar to those traded on Frankfurt's DTB exchange, which would start trading in May.

In a more innovative move, it also launched futures based on the differences between long-term bond yields in Germany and those of France, Spain, Italy and the United States, also poised to start trading in May.
"It's the first stage...in MATIF's preparation for monetary union," chief executive officer and chairman Gerard Pfauwadel told a news conference.

The launch was greeted with some scepticism at the London International Financial Futures & Options Exchange, one of MATIF's main competitors for derivatives business in Europe, along with the DTB (Deutsche Terminboerse).
"We wish MATIF luck but our research suggests that while there is demand for the BOBL (bond) in Germany, we don't feel there's much in Paris," a LIFFE spokeswoman said.

She said the battle for short-term interest rate futures after the launch of a single European currency was as good as sown up, although the struggle for supremacy in long-term interest rate futures was still in the balance.
"We believe we've won the battle for short-term contracts," she said.
Several MATIF members who attended a recent presentation said that while the exchange was now more open to the views of traders than in the past, most reserved judgement on the new contracts.
"People were very reserved. It's not the first time MATIF has launched new contracts," a trader at a U.S. house said.
A trader at a large French bank said the feeling was a bit subdued and downbeat and the failure of five-year futures contracts in past on other exchanges overshadowed the launch.

"Five-year contracts don't tend to work that well and I'm not convinced there's a natural buyer of five-year BTANs. It's not as instinctive a place of reference for the French market," a bond analyst at a French bank said

Pfauwadel said the decision to launch contracts based on German five-year bonds (BOBLs) was driven mainly by the fact that the BOBL option on the DTB was not liquid and MATIF already had a liquid options market in French franc contracts.
"What interested us was not the futures contract but the options contract. The DTB BOBL option doesn't work well. We had to quote the future for technical reasons," Pfauwadel said.
Jacques Werren, MATIF's deputy managing director, said the exchange had consulted the German derivatives exchange and it was "neither enthusiastic nor hostile".

Pfauwadel said the launch of the spread contracts was partly designed to capture Bund futures business from the German and British exchanges and there would be room for intra-European spreads after the introduction of a single currency.

The contracts will be based on benchmarks as close as possible to 10 years for the yield spreads: OAT/Bund (France/Germany), BTP/Bund (Italy/Germany), Obligaciones/Bund (Spain/Germany) and T-Note/Bund (U.S./Germany).
Analysts said the idea was original and could attract some interest in the run-up to monetary union, given the uncertainties about which countries would join and when.
"It's healthy for MATIF to be showing a bit of innovation. It will have a good bit of mileage between now and monetary union but there may not be enough volatility afterwards," one analyst said.
